name: Crab Nebula
desc: The expanding remnant of the supernova recorded by Chinese astronomers in 1054, powered by a central pulsar.
A rich, strongly concentrated globular cluster in Aquarius, one of the larger halo clusters known.
A bright spring globular in Canes Venatici containing several hundred known variable stars.
One of the nearest globular clusters, loosely concentrated with a distinctive central bar of stars, close to Antares.
A very old and luminous globular cluster in Serpens Caput, rivalling M13 in telescopic splendour.

name: Butterfly Cluster
desc: A bright open cluster whose brighter members trace the outline of a butterfly with open wings.

name: Ptolemy Cluster
desc: A large naked-eye open cluster in the sting of Scorpius, recorded by Ptolemy in AD 130.

name: Lagoon Nebula
desc: A giant emission nebula and star-forming region crossed by a dark lane, with the cluster NGC 6530 embedded.
A moderately compact globular cluster near the galactic centre, partly dimmed by interstellar dust.
A bright globular cluster in Ophiuchus forming a well-known pair with M12.

name: Wild Duck Cluster
desc: One of the richest open clusters, its brighter stars forming a V shape likened to a flight of ducks.
A loosely concentrated globular cluster lying about 3° from M10.

name: Hercules Globular Cluster
desc: The finest globular cluster of the northern sky, visible to the naked eye on the western side of the Keystone.
A fairly distant globular cluster requiring moderate aperture to resolve its outer stars.

name: Great Pegasus Cluster
desc: An extremely dense globular cluster with a collapsed core, one of the most concentrated known.

name: Eagle Nebula
desc: A young open cluster within an emission nebula containing the dust columns known as the Pillars of Creation.

name: Omega Nebula
desc: A bright emission nebula whose brightest ridge resembles a swan floating on water.
A sparse young open cluster lying between M17 and M24.
One of the most visibly flattened globular clusters, distorted by its proximity to the galactic centre.

name: Trifid Nebula
desc: A combined emission and reflection nebula divided into three lobes by dark dust lanes.
A small young open cluster just north-east of the Trifid Nebula.

name: Sagittarius Cluster
desc: One of the brightest globular clusters in the sky, easily resolved and visible to the naked eye from dark sites.
A rich, wide open cluster of more than a hundred stars in northern Sagittarius.

name: Sagittarius Star Cloud
desc: Not a true cluster but a window through galactic dust onto a dense star cloud of the Sagittarius-Carina arm.
A bright scattered open cluster containing the Cepheid variable U Sagittarii.
A modest open cluster in Scutum, overshadowed by its neighbour M11.

name: Dumbbell Nebula
desc: The first planetary nebula ever discovered and one of the brightest, showing a clear double-lobed shape.
A compact globular cluster close to Lambda Sagittarii, the lid of the Teapot.
A small open cluster near Sadr whose brightest members form a squat box shape.
A core-collapsed globular cluster in Capricornus with prominent star chains radiating outwards.

name: Andromeda Galaxy
desc: The nearest large spiral galaxy and the most distant object readily visible to the naked eye.
A compact dwarf elliptical satellite of the Andromeda Galaxy.

name: Triangulum Galaxy
desc: A large face-on spiral in the Local Group, notoriously difficult despite its brightness because of its low surface brightness.
A wide, bright open cluster in Perseus, excellent in binoculars.
A rich open cluster at the feet of Gemini, with the smaller distant cluster NGC 2158 nearby.
A young open cluster of hot blue stars, the smallest of the three Messier clusters in Auriga.
The richest of Auriga's open clusters, a dense sprinkling of several hundred faint stars.
A scattered open cluster whose star chains are often described as a cross or the Greek letter pi.
A very loose, nearby open cluster in Cygnus, best seen at low magnification.

name: Winnecke 4
desc: Not a deep-sky object at all but an optical double star; Messier recorded it while searching for a reported nebula.
A bright open cluster about 4° south of Sirius, possibly noted by Aristotle in antiquity.

name: Orion Nebula
desc: The brightest diffuse nebula in the sky and the nearest major star-forming region, illuminated by the Trapezium cluster.

name: De Mairan's Nebula
desc: A detached northern portion of the Orion Nebula, separated from it by a dark lane.

name: Beehive Cluster
desc: A large naked-eye open cluster in Cancer, known since antiquity as a hazy patch between the Aselli.

name: Pleiades
desc: The most famous open cluster in the sky, a young group of hot blue stars wrapped in reflection nebulosity.
A rich, uniform open cluster with the planetary nebula NGC 2438 superimposed on it by chance.
A bright, coarse open cluster forming a striking binocular pair with the fainter M46.
A large scattered cluster long considered a 'missing' Messier object because of an error in the recorded position.
A giant elliptical galaxy, the brightest member of the Virgo Cluster.
A heart-shaped open cluster in Monoceros with a prominent red giant near its southern edge.

name: Whirlpool Galaxy
desc: The first galaxy recognised as having spiral structure, interacting with its smaller companion NGC 5195.
A rich, compressed open cluster in Cassiopeia near the Bubble Nebula.
A distant, compact globular cluster about 1° north-east of Alpha Comae Berenices.
A dense globular cluster now known to belong to the Sagittarius Dwarf Elliptical Galaxy, not our own halo.
A large, loose globular cluster that resolves readily even in small telescopes.
A modest globular cluster lying between Albireo and Sulafat in the summer Milky Way.

name: Ring Nebula
desc: The classic planetary nebula, a small bright smoke ring between Beta and Gamma Lyrae.
A barred spiral galaxy in the Virgo Cluster, one of four Messier barred spirals.
An elliptical galaxy in the Virgo Cluster, forming a trio with M58 and M60.
A giant elliptical galaxy paired in the eyepiece with the spiral NGC 4647.
A face-on barred spiral in the Virgo Cluster that has produced an unusual number of observed supernovae.
A bright, noticeably asymmetric globular cluster close to the galactic bulge.

name: Sunflower Galaxy
desc: A flocculent spiral galaxy whose many short, patchy arms resemble sunflower petals.

name: Black Eye Galaxy
desc: A spiral galaxy with a striking dark dust band across the near side of its bright nucleus.
A highly inclined spiral galaxy, one of the three members of the Leo Triplet.
The brightest galaxy of the Leo Triplet, its arms distorted by gravitational interaction.
One of the oldest known open clusters, roughly the age of the Sun and still gravitationally bound.
A southern globular cluster below Corvus, metal-poor and on a retrograde galactic orbit.
A small, metal-rich globular cluster in the base of the Teapot.
A compact core-collapsed globular cluster almost identical in appearance to its neighbour M69.
A loose globular cluster in Sagitta, long debated as a possible dense open cluster.
One of the faintest and most remote globular clusters in the Messier catalogue.
A chance grouping of four faint stars; astrometry shows it is an asterism rather than a physical cluster.

name: Phantom Galaxy
desc: A perfectly face-on grand-design spiral with very low surface brightness, among the hardest Messier objects visually.
A remote, highly concentrated globular cluster far beyond the galactic centre.

name: Little Dumbbell Nebula
desc: The faintest Messier object, a small bipolar planetary nebula on the border of Perseus and Andromeda.

name: Cetus A
desc: A barred spiral and the prototypical Seyfert galaxy, with an extremely luminous active nucleus.
The brightest reflection nebula in the sky, lit by two hot stars north-east of Alnitak.
An unusual winter globular cluster, probably captured from the Canis Major dwarf galaxy.
A dense, compact globular cluster midway between Antares and Beta Scorpii.

name: Bode's Galaxy
desc: A bright grand-design spiral, the dominant member of the nearby M81 group of galaxies.

name: Cigar Galaxy
desc: An edge-on starburst galaxy driven by its interaction with M81, with gas plumes erupting from its core.

name: Southern Pinwheel Galaxy
desc: A bright barred spiral seen face-on, prolific in supernovae and easy from southern latitudes.
A lenticular or elliptical galaxy at the western end of Markarian's Chain.
A lenticular galaxy marking the northern boundary of the Virgo Cluster.
A lenticular galaxy paired with M84, notable for its strong blueshift as it falls through the Virgo Cluster.

name: Virgo A
desc: A supergiant elliptical with a relativistic jet, whose central black hole was the first ever imaged.
A tilted multi-armed spiral, one of the brighter spirals of the Virgo Cluster.
An elliptical galaxy that appears almost perfectly circular, surrounded by a faint extended envelope.
A large spiral whose star formation has been stripped away by the Virgo Cluster's hot intergalactic gas.
A barred spiral that was long listed as a missing Messier object until the identification was resolved in 1969.
A superb globular cluster that would be famous were it not overshadowed by M13 nearby.
A compact wedge-shaped open cluster in Puppis, the southernmost Messier object discovered by Messier himself.

name: Croc's Eye Galaxy
desc: A spiral galaxy with a bright inner starburst ring surrounded by a faint outer disc.
A barred spiral with a distinct inner ring, a member of the Leo I group.
The brightest galaxy of the M96 group, an asymmetric spiral with a dusty disc.

name: Owl Nebula
desc: A round planetary nebula whose two dark interior patches look like the eyes of an owl.
A nearly edge-on spiral on the western edge of the Virgo Cluster, approaching us rather than receding.
A face-on spiral with one notably extended arm, distorted by its passage through the Virgo Cluster.
One of the largest and brightest face-on spirals in the Virgo Cluster.

name: Pinwheel Galaxy
desc: A huge face-on spiral near the handle of the Big Dipper, asymmetric from past interactions.

name: Spindle Galaxy
desc: An edge-on lenticular galaxy with a sharp dust lane; the identification of M102 is historically disputed and some sources treat it as a duplicate observation of M101.
A small fan-shaped open cluster near Ruchbah, the last entry in Messier's own published list.

name: Sombrero Galaxy
desc: An edge-on spiral with a huge bulge and a razor-sharp dust lane resembling a broad-brimmed hat.
An elliptical galaxy in the Leo I group, harbouring a well-studied central black hole.
A large Seyfert spiral with anomalous arms and a water-maser disc used to calibrate cosmic distances.
A loose globular cluster with dark dust patches, the last globular added to the Messier catalogue.
A mottled, nearly edge-on barless spiral close to Merak and the Owl Nebula.
A barred spiral just south-east of Phecda, the most distant galaxy in the Messier catalogue.
A dwarf elliptical satellite of the Andromeda Galaxy, added to the catalogue only in 1966.
